articles.text: There may not have been record breaking attendance at Piedmont’s July 4 parade, but even in the middle of a heat wave, the 57th annual parade still showed why it is one of the best (and oldest) parades in the Bay Area. While the casual observer may have just seen red, white, and blue, subtle changes and adaptations made this year’s parade unlike the previous 56 years. Last year’s parade, 2023, fell on a Tuesday and the parade had a turnout of over 3,500 bystanders and parade entries. This year, a Thursday, saw a high number of parade viewers who were absent apparently all getting a jump on a four-day weekend. Similarly the number of parade entries was noticeably smaller. The presence of excessive heat, with Piedmont temperatures in the 80s, could have also kept parade goers at home just blocks away. For decades, compulsive Piedmonters would place lawn chairs along the parade route as early as 10 days in advance of the parade. Not so this year. True to tradition, some important people led the parade, including Smokey the Bear with Piedmont firefighters, and Piedmont’s police on motorcycles. From there, the fun began with the Zenith New Orleans Parade Band making way for Grand Marshal Gray Cathrall. Grand Marshal Gray Cathrall in Martin Falarski’s 1967 Ford Mustang with Cici Hoover.

articles.text: – David Ashton Imagine that the home next door to you is sold, a developer demolishes the existing structure, and then builds two new homes on the lot. Each home is larger than all other homes on the street, doesn’t conform with city codes, and violates environmental regulations. It seems that shouldn’t be able to happen in Piedmont, right? As it turns out, it can. In December 2023, the city of Piedmont quietly changed the city code, making this scenario possible. In fact, a project very similar to this has just received building permits from the city. A developer from out of the area purchased an empty lot and quietly applied to build two homes on what was once a single-family home lot. These two homes, plus an ADU, appear certainly to fail to comply with numerous city codes, and apparently will be built in a stream setback, likely violating state and city environmental regulations. Residents believe that this project also poses numerous health and safety risks for the community. There are concerns about increased fire risk by nearly doubling the density of homes on a one-way street as narrow as 13 feet wide, which is not up to state fire code standards and is at the top of a wooded canyon. Additionally, there are concerns about hillside stability and streambed erosion given the project’s scope and proximity to the streambed. This new development approval process, called SB9, has been codified by the city of Piedmont to be even more lenient than state standards require. SB9 forces the local city to fast-track multiple family residential development, bypassing the usual public notice and review process. As a result, this project was approved by city planning staff ministerially, and neighbor concerns for health and safety have thus far been dismissed by Piedmont’s’ Planning Department. Lots with certain environmental features are protected by state law and are exempted from fast-tracking under SB9. The lot in issue has such a feature, a stream, in fact one of Piedmont’s protected streams. However, the city has accepted the developer’s assertion that no stream exists, and has ignored evidence presented by the community to the contrary. When city staff were asked if they would consider evidence in order to enable them to work from facts and find the truth, their response was equivocal. If a project which does not qualify for SB9, proceeds under SB9 review without transparency to the community nonetheless, it signals to developers that environmental and safety standards and compliance with even the most basic aspects of city code can be bypassed with little consequence in Piedmont. This is a dangerous precedent to set. articles.text: Major controversy erupts over plans on dead-end street Piedmont City staff members met with a group of concerned neighbors on Friday, July 5, over concerns about a controversial proposed housing project located at 67-77 Wistaria Way. The project, started by property owners Geoffrey Gibson and Kira Mead, seeks to divide the currently vacant lot at 67-77 Wistaria Way into two parcels where the owners will construct a new home on one parcel and a new home as well as an Auxiliary Dwelling Unit (ADU) on the other. Neighbors close to the project claim that the project fails to meet the law’s site eligibility requirements, lot split requirements, non-compliance with objective standards as well as health and safety concerns of neighbors covered by California’s protective easement statutes. The most serious of these accusations is the assertion that the project endangers protected wetlands, as defined by the US Fish and Wildlife Service, and thus should not be eligible for a lot split under state law. The project’s application was approved by the Planning and Building Department on December 27, 2023. Building permits for the project were approved one week ago on July 2, 2024. Neighbors were notified of the construction by mail on Friday, July 5. Construction is expected to begin on Tuesday, July 16. Neighbors close to the project insist that the lot at Wistaria Way meets the state’s criteria of a wetland. They allege that Wildwood Creek and its headwaters traverse this property, a fact they insist is well known to Piedmont residents and public officials, including members of the Planning Department. articles.text: Photo by Jonah Pagenhart Sophia Gilbert as Maria in YMTC’s production of The Sound of Music Youth Musical Theater Company (YMTC) concludes its 19th season with the Rodgers and Hammerstein classic The Sound of Music, running July 19-28 at El Cerrito High School’s Performing Arts Theater. Based on the real-life story of the irrepressible would-be nun Maria and the Von Trapp Family Singers, The Sound of Music is one of the most beloved musicals of all time and has been entertaining and inspiring audiences for over 60 years. The story of love and art prevailing in the face of fear and hatred features music by Richard Rodgers, lyrics by Oscar Hammerstein II, and a libretto by Howard Lindsay and Russell Crouse. The show features a cast of 29 student performers and six student creative apprentices from cities all over the Bay Area. They are led by a team of professional directors, designers, and musicians, headed by Co-Directors Jennifer Boesing and Celeste Kamiya, Music Director David Möschler, and Choreographer Pam Crane. The production features a 30-piece live orchestra, including three student orchestra musicians, playing Robert Russell Bennett’s original Broadway orchestrations. Piedmont High School senior Danielle Zaroukian plays the role of Berthe, one of the girls in the Trapp family. The Sound of Music opens Friday July 19. Performances run for two weekends at El Cerrito High School’s Performing Arts Theater, 540 Ashbury Avenue, El Cerrito. The run includes evening performances at 7:30 p.m. on July 19 and 20 and July 26 and 27, and matinees at 2 p.m. on July 21 and 28. Tickets are available online at www.ymtcbayarea.org or at the door one hour before curtain. Tickets are $17-$38, with discounts for students, seniors, military, teachers, and groups. A talk with local theater artist Becky Potter will be held on Saturday, July 20, at 6:30 pm in the theater lobby. Potter is an expert on Trude Rittmann, a long-time collaborator of Rodgers and Hammerstein, and arranger of the extended vocal sequence in “Do Re Mi.” Piedmont High School senior Danielle Zaroukian.

articles.text: Creativity always involves risk. At some point, you have to take the leap and trust that things will work out. Most of us aren’t naturally inclined to enjoy risk; it feels scary and unpredictable. We like to be in control, but creativity requires stepping into the unknown. Creativity means bringing something new into the world. You might have an idea – a cake, a painting, a robot, an app – but you can’t predict the exact outcome. The cake might flop, the painting might change colors, the robot might malfunction, and the app might solve a different problem than intended. You just don’t know. To embark on any creative act, or to encourage your children to be creative, you have to get comfortable with risk and make it a normal part of life. Some of you may remember the days before cell phones? We used to take risks regularly. I recall planning to meet a friend in London during a study abroad program in my twenties. We had one overlapping night and planned to meet in a specific park at lunchtime. With no contact in between – no cell phones, no regular email – we still managed to meet up. It was a huge risk, but back then, we took risks like this all the time. Today, everything is preplanned and controlled. To spark creativity, we need to practice taking risks. Here are some simple ways to get started: 1. Take a Leap: Jump off a diving board, dock, or boat into a pool, lake, or river. Feel the thrill of the jump. 2. Learn a New Skill: Be a beginner at something new— try a sport or new artistic medium and embrace the learning process. 3. Try New Food: Order something unfamiliar at a restaurant or try a recipe with a new fruit or vegetable 4. Speak Your Mind: At your next social gathering, share your thoughts and opinions, even if it feels uncomfortable. The more that you can practice taking these kinds of small actions that feel slightly risky, the more your nervous system will be prepared for the larger risks required to embark on the creative path. Nina Meehan is a Speaker, Consultant and Workshop Leader with a specialization in the 3Cs: Creativity, Communication and Connection. https://ninameehan. com/ Take a risk and learn something new. articles.text: Instead of eating to live, Malaysians like to flip the script and live to eat. However. most of that eating is done in humble hawker stalls or centers, places that serve cheap, handmade food in a casual setting. Serving favorites such as satay, chicken rice, rojak, roti, and char kway teow, these family-run stalls have earned the honor as being one of the most popular places to grab a quick bite. Prominent in Hong Kong, Singapore, and Malaysia, food hawkers earned their name in the early 1800s, called “street peddling hawkers.” Many people who were left unemployed after WWII began hawking to make ends meet, occasionally roping in children to help. Nowadays, Malaysians will argue tirelessly over their favorite stalls, keeping the rich hawker culture alive. Hawker stalls are much more than a place to grab a quick bite – they are a rich pillar of Malaysian culture. Unfortunately, by the 1960’s hawker stalls fell under continuous scrutinization from the government, with unlicensed hawkers seen as nothing more than a nuisance and a source of traffic congestion. The Municipal Health Officer saw hawker stalls as a health hazard due to often unsanitary conditions in which food was prepared. This led to a large number of bowel complications, further leading to diseases or death. When local law enforcement tried Nonya kueh purchased from a hawker stall in Malacca Chicken rice is an addictive local favorite. taking action by forking out fines and imprisoning hawkers for short periods of time, this did nothing to solve the problems; hawkers went right back to business. A more effective solution needed to be taken and In 1967, two multi-story hawker centers (no longer stalls) were constructed, paving the way for a new era of hawkers. A significant upgrade from the dusty carts on the streets, the centers offered more stability and more space for hawkers. One of the tings my family loves to joke about is that “Malaysian food is the best Singaporean street food.” In recent years, Singapore has become a popular foodie destination for their “diverse range of international delicacies.” While Singapore is often noticed for its “unique hawker culture”, Malaysia and other South-East Asian countries also deserve this recognition. As Malaysians continue their passionate debates over their favorite hawker stalls, they not only honor the rich history and cultural significance of these establishments but also ensure their enduring presence in the modern culinary landscape. The evolution of Malay hawker culture from its early origins to the present day serves as a testament to the resilience, adaptability, and creativity of diverse hawkers who have preserved and enriched Malaysia’s culinary tapestry. While inarguably producing delicious food, hawker stalls deserve to be recognized for the backbreaking work behind the stall. Whether it’s waking up at four a.m. to make popiah skin (a spring roll with both cooked and fresh ingredients), or standing over an enormous wok to fry goreng pisang (fried banana) all day every day in Malaysia’s back-breaking heat, hawkers deserve praise for their work ethic and contribution to the very fabric of Malaysia. The moral of the story is when you find yourself in Malaysia, instead of heading to the Banyan Tree, make your way down to Petaling Street. Daisy Seymour is a Piedmont teen that enjoys writing for The Post. She also wishes her brother would share his goreng pisang. A traditional hawker stall, selling wonton soup and noodles

Prominent in Hong Kong, Singapore, and Malaysia, food hawkers earned their name in the early 1800s, called “street peddling hawkers.” Many people who were left unemployed after WWII began hawking to make ends meet, occasionally roping in children to help. Nowadays, Malaysians will argue tirelessly over their favorite stalls, keeping the rich hawker culture alive. Hawker stalls are much more than a place to grab a quick bite – they are a rich pillar of Malaysian culture. Unfortunately, by the 1960’s hawker stalls fell under continuous scrutinization from the government, with unlicensed hawkers seen as nothing more than a nuisance and a source of traffic congestion. The Municipal Health Officer saw hawker stalls as a health hazard due to often unsanitary conditions in which food was prepared. This led to a large number of bowel complications, further leading to diseases or death. A more effective solution needed to be taken and In 1967, two multi-story hawker centers (no longer stalls) were constructed, paving the way for a new era of hawkers. A significant upgrade from the dusty carts on the streets, the centers offered more stability and more space for hawkers. One of the tings my family loves to joke about is that “Malaysian food is the best Singaporean street food.” In recent years, Singapore has become a popular foodie destination for their “diverse range of international delicacies.” While Singapore is often noticed for its “unique hawker culture”, Malaysia and other South-East Asian countries also deserve this recognition. As Malaysians continue their passionate debates over their favorite hawker stalls, they not only honor the rich history and cultural significance of these establishments but also ensure their enduring presence in the modern culinary landscape. The evolution of Malay hawker culture from its early origins to the present day serves as a testament to the resilience, adaptability, and creativity of diverse hawkers who have preserved and enriched Malaysia’s culinary tapestry. While inarguably producing delicious food, hawker stalls deserve to be recognized for the backbreaking work behind the stall. Whether it’s waking up at four a.m. to make popiah skin (a spring roll with both cooked and fresh ingredients), or standing over an enormous wok to fry goreng pisang (fried banana) all day every day in Malaysia’s back-breaking heat, hawkers deserve praise for their work ethic and contribution to the very fabric of Malaysia. The moral of the story is when you find yourself in Malaysia, instead of heading to the Banyan Tree, make your way down to Petaling Street. At some point, you have to take the leap and trust that things will work out. Most of us aren’t naturally inclined to enjoy risk; it feels scary and unpredictable. We like to be in control, but creativity requires stepping into the unknown. Creativity means bringing something new into the world. You might have an idea – a cake, a painting, a robot, an app – but you can’t predict the exact outcome. The cake might flop, the painting might change colors, the robot might malfunction, and the app might solve a different problem than intended. You just don’t know. To embark on any creative act, or to encourage your children to be creative, you have to get comfortable with risk and make it a normal part of life. Some of you may remember the days before cell phones? We used to take risks regularly. I recall planning to meet a friend in London during a study abroad program in my twenties. We had one overlapping night and planned to meet in a specific park at lunchtime. With no contact in between – no cell phones, no regular email – we still managed to meet up. It was a huge risk, but back then, we took risks like this all the time. Today, everything is preplanned and controlled. To spark creativity, we need to practice taking risks. Here are some simple ways to get started: 1. Take a Leap: Jump off a diving board, dock, or boat into a pool, lake, or river. Feel the thrill of the jump. 2. Learn a New Skill: Be a beginner at something new— try a sport or new artistic medium and embrace the learning process. 3. Try New Food: Order something unfamiliar at a restaurant or try a recipe with a new fruit or vegetable 4. Speak Your Mind: At your next social gathering, share your thoughts and opinions, even if it feels uncomfortable. The more that you can practice taking these kinds of small actions that feel slightly risky, the more your nervous system will be prepared for the larger risks required to embark on the creative path. articles.text: Recent Piedmont High graduate Jackson Violich has a chance to represent his country on the main stage. After helping the Oakland Strokes Youth 8 boat finish third at the National Championship in Sarasota, Florida, Violich received an invitation to the U.S. Junior National Team as they train for the 2024 World Rowing Under 19 Championships in St. Catharines, Canada from August 18-25. Violich received invitations for both the Youth 8 and Youth 4 boats. “I was elated. It’s definitely a huge opportunity and something I’ve been working toward for a long time,” Violich said. Violich recently competed in Florida at the U.S. Rowing Junior National Championship against hundreds of other athletes, becoming a member of one of the best teams in the country. “It was such an accomplishment. I’m just super proud of everyone at Oakland Strokes; it’s really been my home. There are so many amazing people and friends I’ve met there. It’s a life-changing program and experience as a rowing coming through Oakland Strokes. It was great to show our speed and the work we’ve been putting in,” Violich said. The World Rowing Championships is one of the most prestigious events in the sport. It includes athletes from all over the world, giving youth rowers at a step above their usual competition on the local scale. “It’s super big. Countries from around the world send their top athletes through their own rigorous selection process. It’s international competition, so it’s a cut above some of the racing I’ve been used to. It’s a huge competition,” Violich said. Getting invited to training Jackson Violich will have a chance to earn a spot on a United States boat for the 2024 World Rowing Under 19 Championships. Jackson Violich, PHS Class of 2024, recently received an invitation to train with the U.S. Junior National Team. meant Jackson turned heads in racing events but also during individual workouts. “I think a lot of it comes down to race results and boat-moving scale. Another contributor is speed on the rowing machine, I think my power to weight ratio is pretty good as a lightweight, so I have a lot of potential to move the boat really well,” Violich described. Violich now travels to Chula Vista in Southern California for the start of training. “We’re looking at rowing as much as possible. We’ll be doing a 20-25k row in the morning, a lifting and core session in the afternoon, and probably more rowing on the machine in the evening,” Violich said. Still looking to bring his rowing talents to a college campus, Violich is taking his time on college decisions. Now earning a U.S. Junior National Team invitation, it’s clear any college would hit a jackpot by winning the sweepstakes for his services. articles.text: Tryouts for Piedmont Swim Team, Piedmont’s year round swim team, will take place on August 13-15 at Montclair Swim Club in Oakland. This will be a 3-day tryout, where each swimmer will be given a 30-minute time slot and grouped by age. The expectation is that everyone who tries out will attend all three days. Tryout expectations include the following: Swimmers age 8 and under Swim 25 yards of Freestyle (with side breath) and 25 yards of Backstroke. Legal Breaststroke and Butterfly are not required but are helpful. Swimmers age 9-11 Swim a 50 Freestyle (with side breath), a 50 Backstroke, a 25 Breaststroke (with a legal kick), and a 25 Butterfly with basic stroke mechanics. Swimmers age 12 and older Swim a legal 200 IM with proper breathing mechanics. Swimmers should be able to complete the 200 IM in under 5 minutes. If interested and for more information email joinpst@ piedmontswimteam.org.

Wednesday, July 10, 2024 13 Compiled by Jonathan Comeaux The summer workout series returns for its 17th year. High school athletes as well as current and former college athletes are asked how they stay in shape during the offseason. Aspiring high school and college athletes might gain some insight, as might some armchair quarterbacks. Send us suggestions of athletes you would like to see profiled in the Post this summer. Make sure you give us the person’s name, sport, phone number and e-mail address. Send your information to news@piedmont-post.com. NATALIA MARTINEZ Basketball Jack Stein is set to start his junior year at Pomona-Pitzer, whose team won last year’s Div. 3 NCAA cross country championship. He was the Post’s 2022 Co-Athlete of the Year. JACK STEIN Cross County, Track & Field Piedmont High Class of 2022 Pomona-Pitzer Class of 2026 Jack Stein, PHS Class of 2022, just concluded his sophomore season on Pomona-Pitzer’s cross country and track teams. Last November, Stein helped the Sagehens defeat Wisconsin La Crosse by just one point, 158-159, to claim the Division 3 NCAA National Championship. The former Highlander star finished as Pitzer’s fifth-best runner. His time of 25:49.3 ultimately was what they needed to win the title. He traveled home to Piedmont for Thanksgiving break to run in the 2023 Piedmont Turkey Trot, a 5k street race, and won with a time of 15:30, a course record. In track, Stein closed the season by finishing 50th of 104 in the Occidental Invitational on May 4 with a time of 15:01.20 on a 5k course. He was also seventh of 16 in the 3,000 meter Steeplechase at the 2024 SCIAC Championships on April 27-28. Stein graduated from Piedmont as the school’s all-time record holder in the 1600 and 3200 meters with respective times of 4:14.77 and 9:12.62. He also won the WACC Cross Country championship with a time of 15:34.76, was second of 144 in the NCS Championship in 15:29.4 and placed 12th of 209 at the CIF Championship, clocking a 15:43.4. What is your workout program this summer? I am currently going into my junior cross country season for Pomona-Pitzer. For distance runners, training is measured in miles. Summer training usually includes a slow build in “weekly mileage” until said runner returns to school in the fall where they will have reached “peak mileage”, a weekly mileage that they can maintain throughout the school year and competition. The characteristics of this are specialized to each runner’s goals, injury history, and physiology. For me, I have slowly been building my mileage with the goal of peaking around 85 miles a week in early August. This mileage is primarily done at “easy pace” or a pace that one could hold a conversation at while running. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My goal for this summer is to build what runners call a strong “base”. Fall victories are won on fitness built during the summer, and if you can stay consistent and put in the mileage during the summer, you are setting yourself up for success during the regular season. How are you measuring your development? For distance running, measuring development is easy as you have numbers like weekly mileage and race times to refer to. While this is useful, listening to how my body is feeling is an even better indicator of fitness for me. Numbers are useful, but if relied on too heavily, it can lead to injury. Taking breaks and resting when I feel tired or beat down is super important in ensuring that I don’t burn out on training during the summer. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I am currently working with my coach, Emma Delira, to keep in touch about how my training is going. She was recently named USTFCCCA Men’s West Region Outdoor Track & Field Assistant Coach of the Year. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? In fall 2023, I competed at Division 3 Cross Country Nationals and helped win an NCAA National Championship with Pomona-Pitzer. This spring, I set a personal record in the 5k, running 14:26 at the Occidental Distance Carnival. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? As an athlete at PHS, the best piece of advice I received was “consistency is key”, a phrase that my coach Jeanine Holmlund (Coach B) always emphasized. Especially in distance running, if an athlete can be consistent with their training and set goals, they will improve regardless of their starting point or athletic background. Another piece of advice I would give is to have fun; training is so much easier when you don’t make it a chore, so make sure you are enjoying it. Piedmont High Class of 2024 San Diego State Class of 2028 Natalia Martinez recently graduated from Piedmont High and is embarking on her freshman year on San Diego State’s women’s basketball team. We named Martinez The Posts’ Athletes of the Year in 2024 and 2023, becoming our publication’s first-ever candidate to receive back-to-back Athlete of the Year awards. Martinez led the PHS women’s basketball team to a 20-8 overall record and 7-1 league record to split this year’s WACC title with Bishop O’Dowd, marking Piedmont’s second consecutive league banner. In a 40-point performance against San Leandro, Natalia also set a school record by scoring 10 3-point shots without missing. Natalia won her second straight WACC Player of the Year award and was elected to the SF Chronicle’s All-Metro first-team for the second time. CalHiSports named her to the second-team Open Division. She is one of Piedmont’s highest scorers of all time alongside Courtney Paris, Ashley Paris, Casey Morris, and Trinity Zamora. She concluded her high school career as a four-year starter and never missed a game since coming to Piedmont in 2020. She received our end-of-year awards in each year of her high school career; winning our 2021 Freshman of the Year, 2022 Sophomore of the Year, and our 2023 Athlete of the Year as a junior. What is your workout program this summer? Here’s my workout program: 5:00 a.m.; individual shooting workout, make 250 shots. 9:00 – 10:20 a.m.; Team workouts. 10:30 – 11:30 a.m.; Weight Lift. 11:35 a.m. – 12:00 p.m.; Recovery stretching/ice baths. 3:00 – 4:00 p.m.; Individual dribbling and finishing workouts. What are your fitness goals for the summer? My fitness goals for this summer are to get stronger and maintaining muscle throughout the season. How are you measuring your development? I measure my development by keeping track of the weight I use every time to squat and bench. Typically each week I try to add a little more weight than the week before. A trainer? I left to college on June 14 to start team workouts but I still try to find the time to try to get individual workouts and work with one of the school’s trainers. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? A recent milestone I accomplished is getting my first college practice done. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Find a routine that works for you and stick to it every day. Also, prioritize recovery. JULIEN LEE Cross Country, Track & Field Piedmont High Class of 2024 Colorado College Class of 2028 Julien Lee, PHS Class of 2024, was a four-year varsity member of the school’s cross country and track teams. He’s set to continue his running career at Colorado College in Colorado Springs. Most recently, Lee wrapped up his track and field season by finishing eighth of 24 in the 3200 at the NCS Meet of Champions in 9:55.89. He recorded a personal record of 9:40.94 in the prestigious Sacramento Meet of Champions earlier in the season, finishing 11th of 24. Last fall Lee finished the NCS Championship 27th of 140 runners in 16:57.2. What is your workout program this summer? I have a program from my college coach detailing running and strength workouts. I’m running six days a week and lift three days a week. What are your fitness goals for the summer? I’m just trying to have a solid base for cross country in the fall, so I’m focused on slowly increasing my mileage and strength. How are you measuring your development? I’m not measuring any specifics in these workouts, but I’m doing similar work to previous summers so I know I will be where I need to be by the end of the summer. Are you working on your own? With a coach? A trainer? I’m getting my workouts from my coach through a spreadsheet but I’m mostly running on my own. What is a recent milestone that you have accomplished? I had a good track season in which I ran 4:29 in the 1600 and 9:40 in the 3200. Since then, I’ve mostly been training but I did run a trail race and. placed third. What advice would you offer younger, aspiring, student athletes? Be patient. Whatever sport you participate in, you have a long season and hopefully a long career. It’s easy to get frustrated if you’re not hitting your goals right away, but you have to stay consistent and the results will come eventually. articles.text: Mark Cavendish breaks record for stage wins Photo courtesy of Bicycling.com Tadej Pogačar continues on top with the Yellow Jersey through Stage 10. Reaching the halfway mark of the 2024 Tour de France, twotime champion Tadej Pogačar continues to wear the Yellow Jersey as the leader in the General Classification standings through Stage 10. Pogačar has a 33-second advantage over Remco Evenepoel while back-to-back champion Jonas Vingegaard of Team Visma remains in third place, one minute and 15 seconds back. Aside from Pogačar staying in first, the largest headline of the past week came at the end of Stage 5. Veteran Mark Cavendish, 39, came across the line in first place, marking the 35th stage win of his nearly 20-year career. He broke Eddie Merckx’s 34-year-old record. “I’m in a bit of disbelief. My team took a big gamble letting me come in to try and win one stage. You have to go all in and we’ve done it. We did exactly what we wanted to do, every little detail has been put toward specifically today. We’re not going to be at the top of the rankings, but the Tour de France is bigger than cycling,” Cavendish said following the historic moment. Another bit of exciting news is Walnut Creek native Matteo Jorgenson has entered the top-10 of the general classification standings in 10th place. He’s a teammate of Vingegaard and will likely be pushing the Dane to the finish. It’ll be interesting to see how their team’s strategy develops. This morning, Stage 11 marks a critical day on a 211 km mountain course from Évaux-les-Bains to Le Lioran with six categorized mountains. By the time we return, Le Tour will pass through flat courses in Stages 12-13 of 204 km and 171 km before taking a turn up the Pyrenees to Pau. Stages 14-15 provide 350 km of mountain riding. Stage 14 has three steep climbs, including 19 km up Col du Tourmalet which will have a pair of 9 percent gradient climbs. Stage 15 comes on Bastille Day, July 14 and has five mountain climbs and a 15.8km summit finish up Plateau de Beille. When we return on Wednesday, July 17, things won’t let up with a 177.8 km mountain stage from Saint-Paul-Trois-Châteaux to SuperDévoluy. It features three consecutive categorized mountains including a summit finish. The United States finished third in the 2020 Olympics’ medal count with six, while China won with 11 medals and four goals, and Russia finished second with 10 medals. Here are some events and names to keep an eye on next month. Women’s All-Around Leading the team is Simone Biles, now 27. She made headlines after withdrawing from the Tokyo Olympics four years ago to deal with mental health issues, enabling teammate Sunisa Lee to take the Individual All-Around Gold. Biles comes in with gold medals in the all-around, balance beam, and floor exercise categories at the 2023 World Championships in October. She also took first in all-around and floor exercise at the U.S. Olympic Trials in June. articles.text: [Updated from August 2021] With the summer in full swing, we delve into our third of five features of trails near Lake Tahoe. This one is about the lengthy but awe-striking Rubicon Trail around Emerald Bay. There is currently a fire near Truckee. The Royal Fire at 168 is about 45 miles away from the Rubicon Trail. Be sure to always be aware of your surroundings and remember your way back to your car. The Rubicon Trail is a 5.9 mile out-and-back (11.8 round trip, 1,350 feet in elevation gain) trail that stretches around Emerald Bay with a 360-degree view of Fannette Island, enabling hikers to see the historic Vikingsholm mansion through the quant and quiet Emerald Bay Boat Camp, with countless places to rest beside the crystal blue water on the way to the Rubicon Point Lighthouse. Starting from the parking lot in the Upper Eagle Point Campground, the Rubicon Trail goes 1.6 miles beside Lake Tahoe with before reaching Vikingsholm – a 38-room mansion built in 1929 on the shores of Emerald Bay. It was the summer home of Mrs. Lora Josephine Knight. She inherited her fortune from the passing of her former husband William Henry Moore, whose law firm had controlling interests in United States Steel, Union Pacific, Rock Island Railroad and the National Biscuit Company (later named Nabisco). She was among the primary financial backers of Charles Lindbergh’s trans-Atlantic flight in 1927. Resting on top of Fannette Island is the famous Tea House Knight had constructed when her mansion was finished. The trail continues beside the white sandy beach along Emerald Bay to the northern portion of the Rubicon Trail. It means you’re finally past the exhaustive foot traffic you’re bound to encounter around Vikingsholm. The northern section of the Emerald Bay gives visitors a much more private look of Fannette Island with spots along the shoreline to cool off on a hot day. It leads to the Emerald Bay Boat Camp a mile from the mansion, a secluded $30 per night boat-in campground. Less than a mile from the Emerald Bay Boat Camp entrance is another private unnamed cove with crystal blue water after you The Rubicon Trail walks past the Vikingsholm mansion, created in 1929 by Lora Josephine Knight, who also arranged the construction of her personal Tea House on Fannett Island.

articles.text: Festival Napa Valley The iconic symphonic and orchestral Festival Napa Valley is underway, and tickets are still on sale for individual nights through July 21. The summer festival pairs innovative classical, jazz, contemporary, opera, and dance productions with Napa Valley’s unparalleled food and wine scene. “We present dazzling talent on spectacular stages surrounded by the incomparable beauty of Napa Valley,” said Festival President and CEO Richard Walker. “It’s a one-of-a-kind experience and a highlight of the year for guests and artists, both returning and new.” Performances take place on the Festival Napa Valley Stage at Charles Krug Winery in St. Helena, the Ecolab Theatre and Jackson Family Wines Amphitheater at CIA at Copia in Napa, Nickel & Nickel in Oakville, and at wineries, resorts, and estates throughout Napa Valley. Now in its 18th season, the festival began on July 6 with a concert by musicians from The Frost School at Festival Napa Valley’s Blackburn Music Academy. The Academy is an immersive summer conservatory for emerging professional instrumentalists in the idyllic setting of Napa Valley, and is led by a distinguished core faculty of musicians from The Frost School of Music at the University of Miami and leading orchestras and institutions. “We welcome locals and visitors to enjoy the best days of summer,” said Robin Baggett, Chairman of the Festival’s Board of Directors. “We are thrilled to provide exceptional programming and food and wine events that showcase the very best of Napa Valley.” Visit ht t ps://festivalnapavalley.org/calendar/festival-live-frost-recital-0706/ for full programming and to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Jan Bijvoet in Embrace of the Serpent Know first that Embrace of the Serpent was nominated for an Oscar for Best Foreign Language film from Colombia. Written and directed by David Gallego and filmed in black and white, it is set in the heart of Colombia’s Amazon rainforest. Its images are luminous, the scale of its expansive beauty breathtaking. As well, it possesses a depth of melancholy that is unrelenting, for above all it is an allegory. It is also a tribute to the indigenous people of the Amazon whose voices are now silent and whose cultures have vanished like so much mist on the swirling jungle rivers. The film opens in 1909 on a German ethnographer, Theo (based on the diaries of real life explorer Theodor Koch-Grunberg), portrayed by Jan Bijovet. Deathly ill, he convinces a young shaman, Karamakate (Nibio Torres), to take him up river in search of a plant, the yakruna, which is thought to have healing properties. Karamakate is at first reluctant for inside he rages at the rubber barons who have decimated his tribe and the ecosystem of the forest. Theo convinces him that if he will act as their guide he will show him where his people, called the Cohiuano, are, insisting they still exist. Karamakate agrees, and so with Theo’s river Sherpa, the three men begin their journey in a dugout canoe in search of the sacred plant. It is a trip that takes them into Joseph Conrad’s Heart of Darkness. One of the most unsettling moments of the film occurs at a mission where a priest has taken in a group of orphan boys, their parents killed in the rubber plant wars. But Theo finds that the father is physically abusive and regards his charges as pagans, beating them remorselessly. Running parallel to the story of Theo is that of Evan (Brionne Davis), based on the American botanist Richard Evans Schultes, who, using Theo’s diary and sketches, is also in search of the elusive plant, interested in its medicinal properties. Whether it was the circus or serious music…it didn’t matter to him. Our scene is a dusty frontier town of the old wild West. A cowboy goes into his favorite saloon, expecting to hear some honky-tonk piano and enjoy some liquid refreshment. He goes through the swinging doors and sees a sight that he has never seen before. There are rows of chairs set up theater style. The audience is sedate and dressed in their Sunday best. The cowboy is confused, but he pretends otherwise. He is told that he has to pay for the concert. This is OK with him. The concert is produced by PT Barnum, so it must be a good show, he figures. The first thing that the cowboy sees is a shiny concert grand piano rather than a honky-tonk upright piano. The show appears to be some type of a variety show. There’s an actor who introduces the musical acts. A European opera star, a world famous pianist, and the “world’s greatest violinist.” Sounds really interesting. That was the scene throughout the west from about 1840 until the first world war in 1917. PT Barnum knew how to sell concert music. The other promoters followed the same scheme. Ballyhoo always worked. The earliest music in America from 1500 until 1840 was confined to church music. There were musicales in the homes of wealthy and educated people. articles.text: Coco Chanel created a worldwide brand to include haute couture, perfume and simple black dresses. She resided at the apex of a fashion pyramid, her sense of style and elegance unassailable for decades. Born in 1883 as Gabrielle Chanel and raised by nuns in an orphanage, she managed to overcome the prevailing culture of the time that dictated that women must be linked to men as a mistress or a wife if they were to survive. Unattached women, regardless of their intelligence or abilities, if they were without income, found themselves adrift and at the mercy of harsh economic forces. The film Coco Before Chanel follows Chanel from her very early years to that defining moment when a long line of elegantly dressed women walk down a long staircase wearing her designs as those in attendance applaud. While Chanel’s rags to riches story may be of interest to those following fashion, a more general audience will find her story only mildly compelling. To be sure, Audrey Tatou is perfectly cast as Chanel, the ingenue, and later as the very individualistic woman who would become a hugely successful designer. And Benoit Poelvoorde is remarkable as Etienne Balsan, rich, prone to decadent largesse, and the man who takes Chanel into his home on a sprawling horse farm just outside of Paris. The most interesting and complex aspects of Chanel’s story reside with the emergence of her creative vision – from the tentative design of women’s hats, clothing, and later high fashion. Unfortunately, that period of her life is taken up far too close to the end of the film. Just when Chanel begins to explore her passion for style and her completely revolutionary view of women’s fashion, the film ends. For reasons that are not obvious, the filmmakers spend an inordinate amount of time focusing on her relationship with Etienne and later Arthur Capel, portrayed by Alessandro Nivola, an English industrialist. These are two men with whom she was involved, though neither lends much heat to the story. For Chanel, the heat was in her keen eye for innovation and design. She was an artist, but her art is given short shrift; it should have been the essence of Coco Before Chanel. Coco Before Cha ne l , Directed by Anne Fontaine. articles.text: Princess Mononoke, the magnificent 1997 feature length animated film by Japan’s Studio Ghibli, is an epic story set in Medieval Japan during its ironage period. A world order, so to speak, is in transition: the balance between the forces of nature and those trying to bend the natural world to their own purpose is in conflict. However, animator/ director/storyteller Miyazaki often blurs the lines between good and evil, creating a sense of compelling ambiguity. In this narrative humans, forest animals and nature gods struggle for their share of the changing order. The film opens with a watchtower guard spotting “something wrong in the forest.” Out of this disturbance leaps a remarkable creature, a kind of boar-monster with flesh made of snakes. It attacks the villagers. Riding to their defense comes Ashitaka (Billy Crudup), a young prince of an isolated people. He is encouraged to begin a journey west and try to discover what the source of the disturbance is. He rides a Yakkuru, a beast that is part horse, part antelope and part goat. A scene from Studio Ghibli’s Princess Mononoke He finally arrives in an area prowled by Moro (Gillian Anderson), a hybrid wolf that is also part God. It is then that he sees for the first time a young woman named San (Claire Danes), also known as Princess Mononoke (a spirit of a beast). San is a human child, raised as a wolf, and rides a spirit wolf. The story includes a panoramic trip with extraordinary characters and places, reflecting the deep imagination of Miyazaki. It’s a multilayered, richly told story. But know that for many young viewers, Princess Mononoke is not only complex, but one of Studio Ghibli’s darkest animated films. It may not be accessible or suitable for the little guys. While it is mythical history, to be sure, it also engages, using action and melodrama which will enthrall. The artistry is magical and masterful, qualities that define all of the films of Hayao Miyazaki. Princess Mononoke. Animé by Studio Ghibli. Directed by Hayao Miyazaki. With the voices of Billy Crudup, Claire Danes, Gillian Anderson and Minnie Driver. 2 hrs., 13 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2019. Now streaming on prime/Fandango/ MAX/apple tv.

articles.text: By Chris Honoré Hayao Miyazaki is regarded as one of the most accomplished and award-winning filmmakers in the history of animation. He founded the internationally acclaimed Studio Ghibli in 1985, whose work is revered internationally, most especially in Japan. He won two Academy Awards, and has been the recipient of two nominations, and in 2015 he was awarded a lifetime achievement Oscar. He has also won a BAFTA, A Golden Lion Award for lifetime-achievement, a Kinema Jumpo Award and a Japanese Academy Film Prize. Miyazaki’s filmography is extraordinary and his handdrawn animated films have grossed millions. Princess Mononoke, made in 1999, was outsold at the worldwide box office only by Titanic. Many of his films are considered to be artistic masterpieces while displaying a genius for imaginative storytelling. Born in Tokyo in 1941, he took an early interest in the creation of manga (Japanese comic books and graphic novels) and later animé (Japanese animated shorts and feature films). Miyazaki is today revered in Japan, and coming out of retirement his work continues to be remarkable, as is demonstrated in the recently released, Oscar-winning The Boy and the Heron, now streaming. It will be reviewed in next week’s edition of The Post. Japanese animated film director Hayao Miyazaki, founder of Studio Ghibli

articles.text: Peter Rabbit is based loosely based on the iconic book by Beatrix Potter. This incarnation is a fast-paced, frenetic comedy starring, of course, Peter (James Corden), dressed in his familiar blue coat, always mischievous, who resides on a bucolic farm in the English countryside. He lives a relatively carefree life along with his siblings Flopsy (Margot Robbie), Mopsy (Elizabeth Debicki) and Cotton-tail (Daisy Ridley). This cohort also includes cousin Benjamin Bunny (Colin Moody) and is looked after by the kindly painter, Bea (Rose Byrn). Meanwhile, the denizens of the warren do clash with farmer McGregor (Sam Neil) whenever they raid his vegetable garden. On one particular veggie raid, with Mr. McGregor in hot pursuit, he unexpectedly collapses and fails to get up. It is, of course an unexpected moment; and it sets in motion the essence of the story. Now, in the absence of old Mr. McG, the clan discovers it has the run of the farm, all happily gorging on rows and rows of vegetables. That is until Mr. McGregor’s great-nephew, Thomas (Domhnall Gleeson), moves from London to take over the farm, rehab the aging cottage, all in preparation for a quick sale. Feeling out of his element, he plans a quick return to the city where he will open a toy store. But Peter, of course, has other plans, and so he and his rabbit tribe set out to obstruct Thomas at every turn, intending to sabotage this city slicker’s efforts. Unexpectedly for Peter and crew, Thomas doesn’t retreat but decides that he’s all-in despite the fact that he doesn’t know a rake from a hoe. And thus begins the rabbit vs. city boy scrum over the rights to feed on the veggie garden whenever they please. As it turns out, it was old man McGregor who had captured Peter’s father and alas turned him into a stew. So with a score to settle, and a carrot in hand, Peter, becomes a committed rebel, leaning into battle against another McGregor. Meanwhile, Thomas confides in Bea, telling her he has a “rabbit problem.” Bea in contrast is on the side of the rabbits insisting they are harmless and just part of the local color. But no matter their viewpoints, Thomas does find Bea to be very charming. And so the story goes, riotous at times, and rarely slowing down. Kids will definitely be entertained. Peter Rabbit. Directed by Will Glick. Live action and with CGI. Voiced by James Corden, Faysai Bazzi, Rose Byrn, Doomhnall Gleeson. 1 hr., 35 min. Rated PG. Released in 2018. Streaming on Fandango/ptime/apple tv. articles.text: Sunday, July 21, 4 p.m. PCO Sextet Chamber Concert In a lovely homage to early summer, a skilled sextet of Piedmont Chamber Orchestra musicians will perform a concert called Concentric Circles with music for winds and piano spanning three-quarters of a century. Mostly French or French-inspired, the program includes works by Rimsky-Korsakov, Koechlin, Villa-Lobos, Poulenc, and Milhaud, performed by Martha Stoddard, flute; Jan Davis, oboe; Marcelo Meira, clarinet; Adam Williams, bassoon; Alex Stepans, horn; and Stanley Wolfersberger, piano. The variety of music and combinations of players make this a memorable musical experience. It is free; donations are welcome. Piedmont Center for the Arts strongly encourages proper masking inside the main hall and highly recommends that attendees have all up-to-date vaccinations. Support the programming of Piedmont Center for the Arts by donating generously to the Tip Jar at these events.

It was around 4 pm and the coyote was cruising down Sea View, not the least bit afraid of my big Lab. Fortunately, a woman came by and clapped loudly and the coyote scrammed. Just wanted you and everyone to know. –Cindy and Bad Boy the Lab Dear Cindy and BB: Grrrracious. What’s next? I called Piedmont Animal Services, and they said that because Piedmont is so woodsy, coyotes like it here. They aren’t able to trap coyotes because of Fish & Game’s laws so it’s important to be careful with your cats, dogs, guinea pigs, marmots, parrots or any other creature you love. They did say there’s one coyote that roams around our town that has mange. Be doubly careful around that one. articles.text: It was a sunny, mild afternoon on July 1 for the First Mondays Reading Group. They met outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park with a good turnout of 19 readers. Phil Witte had been at an event promoting his new book, Funny Stuff, How Great Cartoonists Make Great Cartoons. The group wanted to know more, so Phil told them how the book came to be and about the promotional events that are happening. The group was there to discuss Australian author Jane Harper’s 2016 murder mystery, The Dry. It won numerous international awards, has sold more than one million copies worldwide and was the first book in Harper’s Aaron Falk trilogy. A film adaptation of The Dry was released in January 2021 and was one of the highest grossing Australian film opening weekends ever. The novel tells the story of Australian Federal Police investigator Aaron Falk reluctantly returning to his hometown, the struggling farming community of Kiewarra, for the funeral of his childhood best friend, Luke Hadler. The worst drought in a century has created extreme pressure in the community, and it is shocked when the Hadler family is found dead in their farmhouse. Falk and Luke had shared a teenage secret regarding the death of a young friend 20 years earlier, and Luke’s death threatens to bring it back to the surface. The community suspected Falk then, and he doesn’t want to re-engage the townspeople. However, the circumstances around the Hadlers’ deaths, which appear bogged down some readers. They wanted more sustained action and a better understanding of the characters. The inclusion of the long-ago death of Falk and Luke’s friend seemed unnecessary for them, while other readers felt it was a key element of the story. Some members of the group said they weren’t mystery readers, and they don’t enjoy the formulaic complexity of the genre where lots of different possible motives are floated. The reader has to identify which clues are the keys to solving the murder. Other readers liked the twist in the identification of the murderer, but some found it to be a bit of a stretch. One reader regretted there wasn’t complete justice for all the guilty parties, but maybe that’s the way life is too. The Dry may not have satisfied everyone, but the majority of the readers found it a fun, enjoyable summer read. They also said they like the group’s schedule of alternating fiction and non-fiction books. It has expanded the books they read and their reading enjoyment. The group had previously selected Country Girl by Edna O’Brien for August and The Heaven and Earth Grocery Store by James McBride for September. After Lois Price presented reviews of three non-fiction candidates, the readers selected Outliers: The Story of Success by Malcom Gladwell for their October book. Most readers enjoyed Harper’s style and particularly the depth of description she provides. Descriptions of things like flies on rotting corpses certainly provided vivid images for the readers, but this depth of description was also true of Harper’s character development and the story’s setting. The readers agreed the remote geography of Kiewarra and the Australian Outback is a character in the novel. So is the rural, insular, community of Kiewarra’s residents. The draught is central to the story. It is like a vise squeezing the characters and affects what happens. It is a harsh environment in terms of climate, culture, and people. Like Aaron Falk, the group said they wouldn’t want to live in Kiewarra. Some readers did have issues with the book. They found Harper’s storytelling slow and, like Kiewarra, dry. articles.text: Rita Liston, a longtime resident of Piedmont passed away on June 19, 2024. She was 78. Born on a small farm in Mentor, Ohio on May 16, 1946, she was the youngest child and the only daughter of Anna and Frank Juska. Her two older brothers successfully lobbied their parents to name her Rita after watching a film starring Rita Hayworth. Three years later her family moved to Cleveland where Rita graduated from high school in 1964. She attended Ohio University and received her bachelor’s degree in education in 1968. After teaching in Cleveland for a year, she moved to San Francisco where her two brothers were living. Rita’s first and last job in California was at Corvallis Elementary School in the San Lorenzo School District where she taught for over 30 years. Loved and admired by students, staff and parents, Rita taught with humor, enthusiasm and a genuine concern for every student. After retiring in 2008, she was invited to join two honorary societies for educators: Delta Kappa Gamma and Alpha Delta Kappa. She served as an officer in both organizations. Rita was generous in volunteering her time with numerous charities and was passionate about helping children and people in need. Two charities she was especially devoted to were cuddling premature and drug addicted babies at Alta Bates Hospital, and helping Piedmont Community Church settle the Yosufzai refugee family from Afghanistan. Rita formed a close relationship with the mother, Nargis, and was devoted to the Yosufzai children. Rita continued her friendship and support of the family long after they moved from Oakland. In 2007 Rita met Bob Livsey while playing bridge. They fell in love and became life partners in 2008. They both enjoyed traveling and took many wonderful trips together. One highlight of their travels was attending the Democratic National Convention and dancing at one of the Convention Balls while Barack and Michelle Obama were dancing on stage. One lowlight was a bike and barge trip in France. On one very rainy bike day, Bob, the navigator, took a wrong turn despite being in possession of a map and detailed directions to the next barge stop. Rita finally figured out they were on the wrong road, but getting back on track took over two hours in the dark and driving rain. They were the last bikers to arrive at the barge, exhausted and soaking wet. But Rita Liston, a longtime Piedmont resident, died on June 19 at age 78. after changing her clothes and having a stiff drink, Rita (kind of) forgave Bob. Rita had a great sense of adventure and loved to hike with Bob and her beloved dog Molly. During the Covid years Rita discovered a new way to enjoy the outdoors when she came across a book titled “Secret Stairs of the East Bay.” Rita, Bob and Molly completed all 38 walks described in the book, and then moved on to conquer all 21 walks from the “Berkeley Walks” book. This spring she took on the challenge of “Stairway Walks in San Francisco.” Rita’s favorite walk in San Francisco was the beautiful Moraga Stairway in the Golden Gate district which had a special serendipity for her and Bob. But her all-time favorite walk was always Dracena Park where she walked Molly every day. Rita was an avid bridge player and for many years played in two weekly bridge groups. Many lifelong friendships were made over afternoon bridge games and an occasional glass of wine. She also enjoyed her book group, her yoga group, Motown music, crossword puzzles, jigsaw puzzles, and lunch with friends. Rita is survived by her life partner Bob Livsey, her brother Frank Juska and his wife Candace, nephew Andy Juska and his wife Mary, nephew Gabriel Juska, niece Carrie Juska, and two grandnieces Chancey Juska and Maude Juska. She is also survived by loving members of Bob’s family, Scott Livsey, Rachel Livsey and her husband Jeff, Daniel Livsey and his wife Mary, Ben Livsey, and four grandchildren. A Celebration of Rita’s life will be held on Saturday, July 20, 2024 at 2 p.m. at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, CA. In lieu of flowers please consider donating to The Sierra Club Foundation, Feeding America or your favorite charity.

articles.text: A heat wave arrived just before the 4th of July. so the inaugural appearance of the Walking on Wednesdays group in the city’s 4th of July Parade was a hot one. A good holiday week turnout of 34 heat-resistant walkers and one K-9 best friend were on hand for the July 3 walk. Jim Kellogg will lead the walk the following week, and will complete his tour of architectural styles in Piedmont that he started last month. It was hot, so the group planned to stay in the central part of Piedmont to preview the parade route and see their Mesa Avenue assemby spot for the parade. This was going to be the 57th Annual Piedmont Parade, but it was noted that residents of El Cerrito Avenue had mini 4th of July parades during the late 1950s and early 1960s. They were under the leadership of Mary Ellen Sherry and Dorothy Carter, Dick Carter’s mother. Dick and current Piedmont Parade Mistress of the Microphone Patty Edmonds were kid participants in them. The walk began with a look at the Police Department in the lower level of the Veterans Memorial Building where construction had started the prior week on a new dispatch center with the demolition of the old one. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers gave the walkers a report saying that he began advocating for a new dispatch center three years ago. The old one was small and inadequate for the city’s current needs. Piedmont voters approved Measure F this March to increase staffing support, and Piedmont’s share of fund from the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 is being used for the construction. The project is scheduled to be completed in March 2025. Walkers were told that the area above Oakland Avenue was a bit of bohemian neighborhood in the early 20th Century. Jack London lived there, but before him land developer Frank C. Havens was a resident in the area in the late 19th and early 20th Centuries. The house at the corner was built in 1898 and might have been an early office for Havens. Many of the homes in this neighborhood were built soon after the San Francisco Earthquake inn 1906. After Piedmont became a city in 1907 home construction boomed. These streets were part of Wickham Havens’ (Frank C.’s son) Alta Piedmont Track and Alta Heights development. The walkers went on Highland to Moraga Avenue and up to Mesa Avenue, the deignated assembly area for the group’s parade entry. They continued on Mesa to Pala Avenue, and back to Oakland Avenue for their return to the Exedra. Some walkers continued on a loop on Highland to Sheridan and Caperton Avenues, and to a hidden path to Guilford Road. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join. and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Registration can be done at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Among those participating with the Walking on Wednesdays group last week were Karin Fetherston, Bob Wong, Peggy Shultz, Jim Kellogg, Ken Hubbert, Chuck Oraftik, Garrett Clifford, Sherry Jacobs (holding the Piedmont Post), Mark Davis and Noemi Alvarado, Avelina Buijs, Albert Chen, Bill Ahern, Pat Keller, Claudine Bach, Dave DeRoche, Greg Slatoff, Lori Austin, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Phil Witte, Alicia Rivera, Jack and Sharona Fischrup, Melba Yee, Eric Behrens, Kat Lang, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Pepper, Larry Olsen, Elizabeth Richter, Mary Carter, Lois Price, Nancy Olsen, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Kathi Roisen who was walking with them for the first time.

On one very rainy bike day, Bob, the navigator, took a wrong turn despite being in possession of a map and detailed directions to the next barge stop. Rita finally figured out they were on the wrong road, but getting back on track took over two hours in the dark and driving rain. They were the last bikers to arrive at the barge, exhausted and soaking wet. But Rita Liston, a longtime Piedmont resident, died on June 19 at age 78. after changing her clothes and having a stiff drink, Rita (kind of) forgave Bob. Rita had a great sense of adventure and loved to hike with Bob and her beloved dog Molly. During the Covid years Rita discovered a new way to enjoy the outdoors when she came across a book titled “Secret Stairs of the East Bay.” Rita, Bob and Molly completed all 38 walks described in the book, and then moved on to conquer all 21 walks from the “Berkeley Walks” book. This spring she took on the challenge of “Stairway Walks in San Francisco.” Rita’s favorite walk in San Francisco was the beautiful Moraga Stairway in the Golden Gate district which had a special serendipity for her and Bob. But her all-time favorite walk was always Dracena Park where she walked Molly every day. Rita was an avid bridge player and for many years played in two weekly bridge groups. Many lifelong friendships were made over afternoon bridge games and an occasional glass of wine. She also enjoyed her book group, her yoga group, Motown music, crossword puzzles, jigsaw puzzles, and lunch with friends. Rita is survived by her life partner Bob Livsey, her brother Frank Juska and his wife Candace, nephew Andy Juska and his wife Mary, nephew Gabriel Juska, niece Carrie Juska, and two grandnieces Chancey Juska and Maude Juska. She is also survived by loving members of Bob’s family, Scott Livsey, Rachel Livsey and her husband Jeff, Daniel Livsey and his wife Mary, Ben Livsey, and four grandchildren. A Celebration of Rita’s life will be held on Saturday, July 20, 2024 at 2 p.m. at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, Piedmont, CA. Walkers survive Piedmont heat wave By Dick Carter A heat wave arrived just before the 4th of July. so the inaugural appearance of the Walking on Wednesdays group in the city’s 4th of July Parade was a hot one. A good holiday week turnout of 34 heat-resistant walkers and one K-9 best friend were on hand for the July 3 walk. Jim Kellogg will lead the walk the following week, and will complete his tour of architectural styles in Piedmont that he started last month. It was hot, so the group planned to stay in the central part of Piedmont to preview the parade route and see their Mesa Avenue assemby spot for the parade. This was going to be the 57th Annual Piedmont Parade, but it was noted that residents of El Cerrito Avenue had mini 4th of July parades during the late 1950s and early 1960s. They were under the leadership of Mary Ellen Sherry and Dorothy Carter, Dick Carter’s mother. Dick and current Piedmont Parade Mistress of the Microphone Patty Edmonds were kid participants in them. The walk began with a look at the Police Department in the lower level of the Veterans Memorial Building where construction had started the prior week on a new dispatch center with the demolition of the old one. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers gave the walkers a report saying that he began advocating for a new dispatch center three years ago. The old one was small and inadequate for the city’s current needs. Piedmont voters approved Measure F this March to increase staffing support, and Piedmont’s share of fund from the American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 is being used for the construction. The project is scheduled to be completed in March 2025. Walkers were told that the area above Oakland Avenue was a bit of bohemian neighborhood in the early 20th Century. Jack London lived there, but before him land developer Frank C. Havens was a resident in the area in the late 19th and early 20th Centuries. The house at the corner was built in 1898 and might have been an early office for Havens. Many of the homes in this neighborhood were built soon after the San Francisco Earthquake inn 1906. After Piedmont became a city in 1907 home construction boomed. These streets were part of Wickham Havens’ (Frank C.’s son) Alta Piedmont Track and Alta Heights development. The walkers went on Highland to Moraga Avenue and up to Mesa Avenue, the deignated assembly area for the group’s parade entry. They continued on Mesa to Pala Avenue, and back to Oakland Avenue for their return to the Exedra. Some walkers continued on a loop on Highland to Sheridan and Caperton Avenues, and to a hidden path to Guilford Road. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join. and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Registration can be done at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. The group was pleased to welcome Kathi Roisen who was walking with them for the first time.
